Revisiting mafic dykes of Bornholm – Implications for Baltica in
supercontinent Nuna at 1.3 Ga
Toni Luotoa,*, Johanna Salminena,b, Karsten Obstc
aDepartment of Geosciences and Geography, P.O. Box 64, Gustaf Ha¨llstr¨ominkatu 2a, FI-00014, University of Helsinki, Finland
bGeological Survey of Finland, P.O. Box 96 (Vuorimiehentie 5), FI-02151 Espoo, Finland
cInstitute of Geography and Geology, F.-L.-Jahn-Str. 17a, D-17487, University of Greifswald, Germany
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: Baltica and Laurentia form the core of the hypothesized Mesoproterozoic supercontinent Nuna in most paleo-
Paleomagnetism geographical reconstructions. Long gaps still exist in the Mesoproterozoic paleomagnetic record of Baltica, and
Mafic dykes different relative configurations for Baltica and Laurentia have been presented.
Baltica
This study presents new paleomagnetic data obtained for mafic dykes on Bornholm (Denmark, southwest
Nuna Baltica). We provide a new 1.326 ± 0.010 Ga Bornholm Group I paleomagnetic key pole (Plat: 06◦N, Plon:
P P r r e o c te a r m oz b o ri i a c n 165◦E, K: 21, A95: 6◦) for Baltica. This pole supports the low-latitude equatorial core of Nuna at 1.33 Ga, where
Kola Peninsula and Northern Norway of Baltica were facing northeastern Greenland of Laurentia.
Based on statistically different magnetization directions with Group I and differences in Nb-Zr-Y systematics,
we propose a separate Bornholm Group II paleomagnetic pole. This undated, poor-quality pole indicates a
paleolatitude of ca. 50◦, possibly reflecting an age difference compared to Group I, accompanied with the
continental drift.
On Bornholm, the wide Listed and Kås dykes of uncertain age yield significantly different paleomagnetic
results compared to the other studied dykes there. In addition, the virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) of these
dykes are 45◦apart from each other. On the basis of similar Nb-Zr-Y systematics with the dykes of the 0.98–0.94
Ga Blekinge Dalarna Dolerite Group (Sweden) and overlapping paleomagnetic data with the high-quality
0.95–0.94 Ga paleomagnetic poles of Baltica, an early Neoproterozoic age for the magnetization is proposed.
The relatively big discrepancy between Listed and Kås VGPs could stem from an unaveraged paleosecular
variation or from a small but significant age difference during rapid plate movements.

12

### page_14
T. Luoto et al. P r e c a m b r i a n R e s e a r c h 367(2021)106444
Baltica (Fig. 14). Despite the big discrepancy between the Kås and Listed
VGPs they both overlap with 0.95–0.94 Ga paleomagnetic poles of
Baltica from central and southern Sweden (Hellstro¨m et al., 2004;
So¨derlund et al., 2005; Elming et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2018) (Fig. 13).
When inverted, the VGP from the Kås dyke overlaps also the 0.48–0.46
Ga poles in the Phanerozoic APWP (Torsvik et al., 2012), but there are
no indication of geological events affecting Baltica for this period.
Since both dykes produce a single VGP, the unaveraged paleosecular
variation (PSV) of the geomagnetic field may explain the big discrep-
ancy between the Kås and Listed VGPs (e.g. McElhinny and McFadden,
2000). Another explanation is a small but significant age difference
(Abrahamsen, 1977; Abrahamsen and Lewandowski, 1995), related to
the possibly later emplacement of the Listed dyke (Abrahamsen, 1977;
Holm et al., 2010). In addition, Baltica’s kinematics through Rodinia
assembly (1.1–0.9 Ga) are dominated by dramatic changes of paleo-
latitude (e.g. Salminen et al., 2009, 2021a) and similar behavior is ob-
tained for Laurentia (e.g. Swanson-Hysell et al., 2021; Evans, 2021).
This behavior has been variably ascribed to the rapid plate tectonics, or
true polar wander (TPW), or their combination (e.g. Evans, 2003; Sal-
minen et al., 2009, 2021a; Swanson-Hysell et al., 2021).
5.3. Correlating the Bornholm dykes with the Precambrian dyke swarms
of southern Sweden

problematic. This is exemplified with the two dyke swarms of southern
Sweden with similar trend, but distinctly different ages, namely the
0.98–0.94 Ga Blekinge-Dalarna Dolerite Group (BDDG) dykes and, the
1.22 Ga Protogine Zone Dolerite Group (PZDG) dykes (So¨derlund et al.,
2005) (Fig. 1).
Here we are using the Nb-Zr-Y systematics as a fingerprint for magma
source since it is rather insensitive to differentiation and secondary
processes (e.g. Fitton et al., 1997; Luttinen, 2018) and compare the data
of the Bornholm dykes (Holm et al., 2010) with the data from the dyke
swarms in southern Sweden (Solyom et al., 1992) (Fig. 12). Variations in
the Zr/Y and Nb/Y values show that the Groups I and II form distinct
trends that are most easily associated with variable degrees of melting in
the mantle source of these rocks. In addition, the Bornholm Group I and
II dykes do not correlate with the BDDG and the PZDG dyke swarms of
southern Sweden, indicating separate sources. According to Solyom
et al. (1992) both the BDDG and the PZDG are generated by low to
moderate degrees of partial melting of a garnet-lherzolitic mantle.
However, the rocks in the PZDG show an alkaline character, whereas the
rocks in the BDDG show a tholeiitic character with majority of rocks
being basaltic andesites.
The different geochemistry together with unusual thickness of the
Listed and Kås dykes may indicate difference in age compared to other
dykes of Bornholm. Nb-Zr-Y systematics of the Kås and Listed dykes
(Holm et al., 2010) are similar to those of some of the similarly striking
dykes of the 0.98–0.94 Ga BDDG in southern Sweden (Fig. 12), which

### page_16

also been presented by Johansson (2009) and Halls et al. (2011)
(Fig. 16). In various Nuna models the Siberia is reconstructed either in a
tight fit with northern Laurentia (Wu et al., 2005; Evans and Mitchell,
2011, Ernst et al., 2016) or located ca. 1500 km from the present-day
northern Laurentia (Pisarevsky et al., 2008; Pesonen et al., 2012). We
show Siberia in a tight fit with Baltica and Laurentia (Fig. 17). The stable
core of Nuna formed by Baltica, Laurentia and Siberia is further sup-
ported by similar drift rates for these cratons at 1.6–1.4 Ga (Elming
et al., 2021). Siberia lacks post-1.4 Ga high-quality paleomagnetic data,
but coeval 1.27–1.24 Ga dyke swarms in Baltica, Laurentia and Siberia
have been suggested to indicate the rifting of the core of Nuna (e.g.
Evans and Mitchell, 2011; Ernst et al., 2016; Elming et al., 2021).
There is also a growing consensus of the proto-SWEAT (e.g., Moores,
1991; Dalziel, 1991, Hoffman, 1991) connection between west Lau-
rentia and proto-Australian cratons (e.g. Zhao et al., 2002, 2004; Rogers
and Santosh, 2002, 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Pisarevsky et al., 2014a;
Pehrsson et al., 2016). It has been proposed that the break-up of Nuna
started with internal displacements within East Nuna, when Mawson
rotated with respect to North and West Australian Cratons (Betts and
Giles, 2006; Pisarevsky et al., 2014a). This was followed by separation of
East Nuna from the core of Nuna. Based on similar Hf and Nd isotopic
compositions in 1.44 Ga granitoids from the Transantarctic Mountains
with ca. 1.5–1.3 Ga Laurentian granites, Goodge et al. (2008) suggested
that Laurentia and East Antarctica (part of Mawson craton) as a part of
proto-Australia were still connected at 1.44 Ga. Pisarevsky et al. (2014a)
proposed that the break-up of Laurentia and proto-Australia could have
been associated with the rift-related 1.38 Ga Hart River magmatism in
the northern part of western Laurentia. However, a recent ca. 1.3 Ga
high-quality paleomagnetic pole from Derim Derim sills (North
Australia) indicates that connection between proto-Australia and Lau-
rentia remained at least until 1.3 Ga (Kirscher et al., 2020). Therefore,
Kirscher et al. (2020) suggested that proto-Australia was part of the core
of Nuna in proto-SWEAT connection for at least 300 million years (ca.
